[1] rewrite

```
- **Why the step-size test allows a 0.5% difference.** No record says how 0.5%
  was chosen. It dates from an earlier, approximate calculation method, whose
  runs differed by about 0.04% in alveolar concentration and by more in
  mixed-venous concentration. The test also requires each gap to stay below
  1e-14 as a fraction. Any gap that breaks 0.5% is at least 1e-8, so it breaks
  1e-14 too. Today the 0.5% limit changes no outcome.
```

[2] rewrite

```
- **How to change the step-size test's limits.** A fork with an approximate
  calculation method fails the 1e-14 limit even when its arithmetic is correct.
  For example, a first-order method shows gaps near 1.4e-11. Relax 1e-14, and
  0.5% becomes the working check. Set it above the method's own gaps at the
  test's time steps and below a difference that a learner could see. The
  constants are in `tests/reference/test_sevo_patient.py`.
```

[3] rewrite

```
**Checking the time step, and why a 0.5% difference passes.** The model
advances in fixed steps of 0.1 s, and a shorter step should give almost the
same result. Before each release, a test reruns the first minute of the default
sevoflurane induction with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. Each run's
alveolar, vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5% of
the run with the next shorter step. In a compartment that holds almost no
agent, a tiny difference is a large percentage, so its two values also pass if
they differ by less than 0.000001 vol%. The 0.5% limit was set for the
simulator's earlier calculation method, at about ten times the 0.04% alveolar
difference that method showed. The current method's runs agree to better than
one part in a trillion (simulated 2026-10-03), so the much tighter limits in
the paragraphs above are the ones that would catch a real error.
```

[4] rewrite

```
The 5e-3 relative tolerance was chosen when the simulator used an earlier
calculation method, the operator split. That method showed a relative gap of
4e-4 in the alveolar fraction between steps of 0.1 s and 0.025 s, and 5e-3 is
about ten times that gap. The tolerance is kept as a coarse check, because the
current method, the exact step, gives gaps of about 1.4e-13 relative in the
same comparison (simulated 2026-10-03). The 1e-8 absolute tolerance lets a
negligible difference pass where a fraction is so close to zero that a
relative gap means little.
```

[5] rewrite

```
**Checking the time step, and why a 0.5% difference passes.** The simulator
moves the model forward in fixed time steps, normally 0.1 s long. A shorter
step should give almost the same result. If it does not, the step is too long.
Before each release, a test runs the first minute of the default sevoflurane
induction three times, with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. In each run,
the alveolar, vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5%
of the run with the next shorter step. In a compartment that still holds almost
no agent, a tiny difference can be a large percentage, so a percentage means
little. There, two values also pass if they differ by less than 0.000001 vol%,
which is one part in a hundred million of the gas. With the simulator's current
calculation method, the three runs agree to better than one part in a trillion
(simulated 2026-10-03), so this test is now only a coarse safety net. The much
tighter limit in the paragraphs above is the one that would catch a real error.

The 0.5% limit was set for the simulator's earlier calculation method. With
that method, the alveolar concentrations of the 0.1 s and 0.025 s runs differed
by about 0.04%, so the limit allowed about ten times that difference. The test
compares each run only with the next shorter step. Under the earlier method,
a direct comparison of the 0.1 s run with the 0.025 s run would have failed.
Their mixed-venous concentrations differed by 0.55%. At one minute, these
concentrations have barely begun to rise.
```

[6] rewrite

```
**The maximum dial settings for the three agents come from two classes of vaporizer.** The
sevoflurane and isoflurane maxima are those of variable-bypass dials. Desflurane's is the top of
the Tec 6's range, and a Tec 6 is a heated gas–vapour blender. The model fixes ambient pressure at
760 mmHg (§ "Assumptions"). At that pressure, the same dial setting on either class gives the same
partial pressure, so the model does not need to know which class a maximum came from. The classes
would differ only at reduced ambient pressure, which is not modelled (§ "Known limitations").
```
